voice: Wholesale-led but readable to homeowners. No call to action - the caption ends on the substance. Specs are stated plainly, never dressed up. Every claim is taken from the spec panel on that product's own artwork and nowhere else: no lumen, IP, lm/W, colour-temperature or warranty figure appears in a caption unless it is printed on the graphic it is attached to.
source: Catalogue supplied 2026-08-25 (drive-download-20260825T190330Z-1-001): 122 products, 178 image files, 13 categories. Imported by scripts/import_catalog.py.
notes: First line is the hook - it is the only text visible before 'more', so it carries the keywords.
Hashtag sets are deliberately varied post to post. An identical block on every upload reads as automation.
No city hashtags are used anywhere. DK's location was never confirmed, and a wrong city pulls the wrong leads. Add them once the city is known.

The 'group' field is a sub-family within a category - bulb-a60, tube-dshape, downlight-smart and so on. It is what the within-block ordering rotates through, so two visually near-identical tiles never land next to each other on the grid.
'category' is the grid block. Blocks are posted whole and in the order set in config/brands.json.
No call to action: DK's captions end on the information itself. Nothing asks the reader to message, DM or click.
Ids are assigned in posting order, dk-001 first. Re-ordering blocks does not require renumbering - build_schedule.py reads the block list, not the ids.

posts.caption:
15W adjustable panel, and a cut-out that moves with you.

The face is 110mm. The cut-out is adjustable from 2in to 4in, which is the specification that matters on a refit: you are not measuring the ceiling to suit the fitting, you are setting the fitting to suit a hole somebody else already made.

120 lm/W. 3000K, 4000K and 6500K, so the same fitting covers a bedroom and a shop counter without changing the order.

600 x 600, 60W, 140 lm/W.

This is the ceiling grid module - the one that drops straight into a standard false-ceiling tile and lights an office without a single visible fitting. 140 lm/W is the highest efficiency in the panel range, which is what you want when there are forty of them on one floor and the bill is monthly.

AC 85-265V. 3000K, 4000K and 6500K.

18W open frame. No visible trim, no bezel.

The open-frame build sits the diffuser flush with the ceiling line, so what you see is a lit circle rather than a light fitting stuck to the plaster. 120mm across, 120 lm/W.

3000K, 4000K and 6500K on the same unit.

20W, 122mm face, cut-out adjustable 2in to 4.5in.

The middle of the adjustable range. Enough output for a living room or a mid-size retail bay, and the same spring-clip cut-out spread as the 15W, half an inch wider at the top end.

120 lm/W. 3000K / 4000K / 6500K.

300 x 1200mm. The long one.

Where a 600 x 600 lights a square of ceiling, this lights a run - corridors, reception desks, the aisle between two racks. 40W at 140 lm/W, and the 1200mm length lines up with the module on most suspended ceilings, so a row of them reads as one continuous line rather than a series of squares.

AC 85-265V. 3000K, 4000K, 6500K.

24W open frame, 164mm across.

The larger of the two open-frame panels. Same frameless build as the 18W - diffuser flush to the ceiling, no trim ring - with a wider face and more output behind it, which suits a hallway or a shop floor where the ceiling is higher than a bedroom's.

120 lm/W. 3000K / 4000K / 6500K.

24W - the widest cut-out in the adjustable range.

150mm face, and the cut-out spans 2in all the way to 6in. That range is the point of it: one part number covers holes left by four different fittings, which is the difference between a refit that needs one box on the van and a refit that needs four.

120 lm/W. 3000K / 4000K / 6500K.

600 x 600 at 50W, for when 60 is more than the room needs.

Same module, same 140 lm/W, ten watts down. On a floor of forty panels that is 400W off the connected load for a difference most people will not see, which is the kind of arithmetic that decides a tender.

AC 85-265V. 3000K / 4000K / 6500K. Wholesale and project rates on full cartons.

30W, IP66, and a die-cast housing that treats heat as the actual problem.

Flood lights do not usually fail because the LEDs wear out. They fail because water gets in, or because nothing carries the heat away from the board. IP66 covers the first. The finned casting covers the second.

3000K, 4000K and 6500K. Two-year replacement warranty.

The bubble lens, and why a flood light has one.

A flat lens throws a hard-edged rectangle with a bright core. The bubble lens over each diode spreads the beam before it leaves the fitting, so the pool of light on the ground is wider and the middle of it is not three times brighter than the edge.

30W, 140 lm/W, 0.95 power factor, AC 85-265V. 3000K and 6500K.

50W over a gate, a yard, or the front of a building.

This is the size most people actually need and the one most people over-buy past. 50W of LED at this efficiency covers a driveway and the wall behind it comfortably; going to 100 mostly buys glare.

IP66. 3000K / 4000K / 6500K. Two-year replacement warranty.

0.95 power factor on a 50W flood.

Power factor is the specification nobody reads on a domestic fitting and everybody reads on a hundred of them. At 0.95 the apparent load stays close to the real one, which keeps the cable and the breaker sized for the light you are actually running.

140 lm/W, bubble lens, AC 85-265V. 3000K and 6500K.

The HLFL 50W - same output, different casting.

Two 50W floods in the range on purpose. The housings differ in depth and fin pattern, which changes what they weigh and how they mount, and on a bracket that was drilled for something else that is the whole decision.

IP66. 3000K / 4000K / 6500K.

100W across a warehouse yard.

At this size the bubble lens earns its keep. Loading bays are worked at night by people carrying things, and a hard-edged beam with a hot centre puts half the yard in contrast shadow. The spread lens trades peak brightness for an even floor, which is the one that stops someone tripping over a pallet.

140 lm/W, 0.95 power factor. 3000K and 6500K.

100W, IP66, two-year replacement warranty.

The warranty is the part worth reading. A flood light mounted eight metres up is not a thing anyone wants to take down twice, so what matters is not the first failure rate but whether someone answers the phone when a batch goes wrong.

Die-cast body, finned for heat. 3000K / 4000K / 6500K.

150W on a billboard, where the light has to land flat.

Sign lighting is unforgiving - a hot spot in the middle of a hoarding is visible from the road and looks like a fault. Bubble lens, mounted low and angled up, spreads the beam across the face instead of burning a bright patch into the centre of it.

140 lm/W, AC 85-265V. 3000K and 6500K.

150W. Factory yards, stadium ends, building facades.

Once past 100W the housing stops being a cosmetic decision. This one is die-cast with a deep fin array because 150W of diode makes real heat, and heat is what sets how long the output holds before it starts dropping.

IP66. 3000K / 4000K / 6500K. Project pricing on quantity.

200W, and still 140 lm/W.

Efficiency usually falls away at the top of a range - more diodes in the same casting means more heat, and heat costs lumens. Holding 140 lm/W at 200W is the useful part of this spec, not the wattage.

Bubble lens, 0.95 power factor, AC 85-265V. 3000K and 6500K.

200W. This is the one that replaces a metal halide.

A 400W halide draws its 400W plus ballast losses, takes minutes to strike, and loses a third of its output over its life. 200W of LED at IP66 starts instantly, restrikes hot, and holds output - and the existing bracket usually takes it.

3000K / 4000K / 6500K. Two-year replacement warranty.

300W. The top of the flood range.

At this size you are lighting a stadium end, a container yard or the whole face of a building, and the questions narrow to two: does the casting move the heat, and does the seal hold through a monsoon. Die-cast and finned, rated IP66.

3000K / 4000K / 6500K. Two-year replacement warranty.

3W. The smallest fitting in the range, and the one that changes a ceiling most.

50mm face, 2in cut-out. At this size you stop thinking about one light and start thinking about spacing - a line of them over a counter, or a grid across an alcove, doing the job one big fitting does badly.

120 lm/W. 3000K and 6500K.

13W COB, 120mm face, cut-out adjustable 3in to 4in.

The largest COB in the range. A chip-on-board emitter puts the whole array behind one lens, so the beam comes out as a single clean cone instead of the several overlapping shadows you get from a cluster of separate diodes.

120 lm/W. 3000K, 4000K and 6500K.

Deluxe 5W - same output, better housing.

65mm face into a 2in cut-out. The difference between this and the standard 5W is the trim and the heat path, not the light: a heavier casting holds the junction cooler, and a fitting that runs cooler holds its colour over its life instead of drifting.

120 lm/W. 3000K and 6500K.

7.5W moveable, with three colour temperatures in one fitting.

3-in-1 CCT means 3000K, 4000K and 6500K are selectable on the unit itself - so a wrong call at specification time is a switch, not a re-order. The head tilts, and the reflector comes in golden, silver or black.

112mm face, 3in cut-out. 120 lm/W.

The Sunflower trim, and the reason it is shaped like that.

The petal ridging around the face is not decoration - it is surface area. More metal in contact with air means the heat behind a 5W emitter has somewhere to go, in a body only 60mm across where there is no room for a conventional fin stack.

2in cut-out, 120 lm/W. 3000K and 6500K.

The back of a 13W COB, which is the half that decides the install.

Spring clips, a driver on a tail rather than moulded into the body, and a finned rear that needs air behind it. That last one is the specification people miss: a downlight packed into insulation runs hot no matter what the box says.

120mm face, 3-4in cut-out, 120 lm/W.

8W into a 3in cut-out.

The middle of the COB range and the one that covers most rooms - brighter than the 5W without the 13W's 120mm face, which matters when the ceiling already has 3in holes in it.

112mm face, 120 lm/W. 3000K, 4000K and 6500K.

5W moveable. Point it, then re-point it next year.

A fixed downlight commits the ceiling to whatever the room was on the day it was wired. A tilting head does not - move the sofa, move the artwork, and the light follows without touching the plaster.

65mm face, 2in cut-out, 120 lm/W. 3000K and 6500K.

Golden, silver or black reflector, on the same 7.5W body.

The reflector is the part that shows once the fitting is in the ceiling, and it is a stock decision rather than a build one - the same unit, three finishes, so a showroom and a shop counter get the look they need out of one line on the order.

112mm face, 3in cut-out, 3-in-1 CCT, 120 lm/W.

7W in, 750 lumens out.

Most downlight specs give you efficiency and leave you to do the arithmetic. This one states the output directly: 750 lm from 7W, cool white at 6500K, into a 112mm cut-out with a 105mm face.

80% energy saving against the incandescent it replaces.

13W, 120mm face, cut-out adjustable from 3in to 4in.

The standard large downlight. One inch of adjustment does not sound like much until you are working under a ceiling somebody else cut, where the holes are 3in in one room and 4in in the next.

120 lm/W. 3000K, 4000K and 6500K.

The Alpha 7W. Nothing clever about it, which is rather the point.

105mm face, 3in cut-out, spring clips, a flat diffuser. No tilt, no colour switch, no sensor - the fewer moving parts a ceiling fitting has, the fewer reasons it has to come back down.

120 lm/W. 3000K, 4000K and 6500K.

13W into a 120mm face - the size a hallway actually needs.

Corridors get under-lit because people space downlights by eye and end up with pools and gaps. A 13W at this face diameter throws wide enough that a run of them overlaps into one even wash rather than a row of bright circles.

Cut-out 3-4in adjustable. 120 lm/W. 3000K / 4000K / 6500K.

7W AK downlight - 112mm face, cut-out 2in to 3in.

The cut-out range is the useful number here. A 2in hole and a 3in hole are two different fittings in most catalogues; this one covers both, which is one box on the van instead of two.

120 lm/W. 3000K, 4000K and 6500K.

PL-Alum 13W. The aluminium is the specification.

A plastic-bodied downlight is cheaper and lighter and holds heat against the driver. An aluminium body moves it out. At 13W in a sealed ceiling void that is the difference between a fitting that lasts its rated life and one that dims early.

120mm face, 3-4in cut-out, 120 lm/W. 3000K / 4000K / 6500K.

10W, 112mm face, 3in cut-out.

The step between the 7W and the 13W, and the one most bedrooms want - enough to light the room properly without the 13W's wider face dominating a low ceiling.

120 lm/W. 3000K, 4000K and 6500K.

The HR 13W - a fixed 3in to 4in cut-out, sized to fit rather than to adjust.

Where the adjustable trims buy flexibility with a spring mechanism, this one is dimensioned to drop into the hole and sit flat. Fewer parts in the trim, and nothing to work loose in a ceiling that gets vibration from a floor above.

120mm face, 120 lm/W. 3000K / 4000K / 6500K.

S-HR 7W. 112mm face into a 3in cut-out.

The smaller HR body. Same fixed-trim approach as the 13W - dimensioned to sit flat rather than sprung to adjust - in the wattage most rooms are actually specified at.

120 lm/W. 3000K, 4000K and 6500K.

Lining Alum 13W - the ribbed body, and what the ribs are for.

Every line down that casting is heat leaving the driver. It is the same reason an engine block has fins: the metal is not thicker, it is folded, so more of it touches air in the same diameter.

120mm face, 3-4in adjustable cut-out, 120 lm/W. 3000K / 4000K / 6500K.

10W behind a 120mm face.

Same output as the 112mm version, wider trim. That is a cover-up specification and a useful one: when a 13W comes out and leaves a 4in hole, a 10W with a 120mm face goes back in without anybody skimming the ceiling.

Cut-out 3-4in adjustable. 120 lm/W. 3000K / 4000K / 6500K.

Star 7W, 105mm face.

Another 7W into a 3in cut-out, and a different trim profile again. The range carries several because the visible ring is the only part of a downlight anyone ever looks at, and matching it to what is already in the ceiling is most of the specification.

120 lm/W. 3000K, 4000K and 6500K.

PL-Alum 13W, specified by its 120mm face.

Worth being precise about, because two numbers get confused on every downlight order: the face is what you see, the cut-out is the hole. This one is 120mm across the visible trim, into a 3in to 4in cut-out.

Aluminium body. 120 lm/W. 3000K / 4000K / 6500K.

7W, 112mm face, 3in adjustable cut-out.

The wider-trim 7W. Seven watts is where most ceilings land once the spacing is worked out properly - people reach for 13W because the room feels dark, when the actual problem is four fittings doing the work of six.

120 lm/W. 3000K, 4000K and 6500K.

The driver, the tail and the clips.

What is behind a PL-Alum 13W once it is out of the box: a separate driver on a flying lead, sprung clips at the trim, and an aluminium can between them. Separate driver matters on a service call - it fails more often than the diodes do, and it is replaceable without pulling the fitting.

120mm face, 3-4in cut-out, 120 lm/W.

S-HR 7W with the 105mm face.

The narrower of the two S-HR trims - 105mm rather than 112mm, into the same 3in cut-out. Seven millimetres is invisible on its own and obvious in a row of six, which is why the range carries both.

120 lm/W. 3000K, 4000K and 6500K.

Alpha 7W, 105mm face, 3in cut-out.

The plainest fitting in the downlight range and the one that moves in cartons. No tilt, no CCT switch, no sensor - which is exactly what a dealer wants stacked on a shelf, because it fits nearly every job that walks through the door.

120 lm/W. 3000K, 4000K and 6500K. Wholesale rates on full cartons.

The Smart 7W in its three-colour version.

Same 105mm face and 3in cut-out as the 6500K-only unit, with 3000K, 4000K and 6500K on the one fitting instead. Which of the two you want is a stock question rather than a lighting one: fixed cool white is cheaper per unit, switchable is fewer part numbers to hold.

120 lm/W.

18W over four feet, in a square batten.

The square profile is the one that sits flat against a ceiling or a wall without a bracket - the flat back is the fixing surface. Four foot is the length that lines up with the old 36W fluorescent it usually replaces, at half the load.

120 lm/W. 3000K and 6500K.

Same 18W, round profile.

A round diffuser spreads light through a wider arc than a square one, so it throws onto the ceiling as well as the floor. In a room with a white ceiling that bounce is what stops the fitting reading as a bright stripe in the dark.

4FT / 1.2m, 120 lm/W. 3000K and 6500K.

The D-shape, and what the flat side is for.

Round tubes need a cradle. A D-profile has one flat face, so it mounts straight onto a surface and the curved half does the diffusing. Fewer parts, and nothing between the fitting and the wall to collect dust.

20W over 2FT / 0.6m. 120 lm/W. 3000K and 6500K.

T5, 9W, two foot.

T5 is a diameter, not a brand - the slimmest of the standard tube profiles, which is why it ends up under kitchen cabinets and inside display cases where a T8 will not fit.

2FT / 0.6m, 120 lm/W. 3000K and 6500K.

The tube rod - a bare 18W tube, no batten.

This is the replacement lamp rather than the whole fitting. Where a batten brings its own housing and driver, a rod goes into the channel that is already on the ceiling, which is the cheaper half of a refit if the housing is sound.

4FT / 1.2m, 120 lm/W. 3000K and 6500K.

40W in a four-foot square batten. High power.

Double the usual 4FT wattage in the same length, which is a workshop and warehouse specification rather than a domestic one - places where the ceiling is six metres up and the light has to arrive with something left in it.

120 lm/W. 3000K and 6500K.

IP65, 40W, four foot. The one that goes where water does.

Sealed end caps and a gasketed body, so it takes a wash-down or a covered outdoor run without the tube filling with condensation. Car park soffits, kitchens, poultry sheds, anywhere a hose gets pointed near the ceiling.

120 lm/W. 3000K and 6500K.

T8, 12W, two foot.

T8 is the fat one - the diameter nearly every fluorescent batten in the country was built around. Which makes it the retrofit size: the existing housing takes it, and the only thing that changes is the load.

2FT / 0.6m, 120 lm/W. 3000K and 6500K.

9W, two foot, round. Project and contract pricing.

The small round batten is the one that goes out by the hundred - stairwells, service corridors, back-of-house. At that volume the unit price stops being a list price and starts being a conversation.

2FT / 0.6m, 120 lm/W. 3000K and 6500K.

40W D-shape over four feet.

The top of the D-profile range. Surface-mounts flat like the smaller ones, with workshop output behind it - one of these over a bench does the job two 18W battens were doing, on one fixing instead of two.

4FT / 1.2m, 120 lm/W. 3000K and 6500K.

12W, two foot, square batten.

The short square. Two foot is the length that fits over a doorway, inside a wardrobe, or along the back of a shop shelf - places where a four-foot batten is simply too long and gets cut about on site.

2FT / 0.6m, 120 lm/W. 3000K and 6500K.

T5 at four foot, 18W.

The long T5. Same slim diameter as the one-footer, stretched to 1.2m, which is what goes into cove details and behind pelmets where the fitting has to disappear into a 40mm gap.

120 lm/W. 3000K and 6500K.

9W tube rod, two foot.

A bare replacement tube for a housing that already exists. Worth checking one thing before ordering: whether the old fitting has a starter and a ballast still wired in, because those come out, not just the lamp.

2FT / 0.6m, 120 lm/W. 3000K and 6500K.

40W, four foot, round profile. High power.

The round diffuser at full output. Round throws wider than square, so in a warehouse aisle a run of these lights the racking either side as well as the floor between - which is the difference between finding stock and hunting for it.

120 lm/W. 3000K and 6500K.

10W over a foot and a half.

The odd length in the range, and a useful one. 0.45m fits the gap above a kitchen worktop between two wall units, where a 1FT is mean and a 2FT does not clear the cupboard.

D-profile, surface mount. 120 lm/W. 3000K and 6500K.

T8, 24W, four foot.

The straight swap for a 36W or 40W fluorescent tube, at roughly half the draw and with no starter, no ballast hum and no ten-second flicker before it settles.

120 lm/W. 3000K and 6500K.

20W in a two-foot batten. High power.

Twenty watts is a lot for 0.6m - this is the short batten specified for output rather than for fitting a gap. Over a workbench or a till it puts down more light per foot than anything else this size in the range.

120 lm/W. 3000K and 6500K.

9W, two foot, square.

The quiet one in the range. Not the brightest 2FT and not meant to be - 9W is what a corridor, a landing or a storeroom actually needs, and specifying 20W there just costs money and makes the space glare.

120 lm/W. 3000K and 6500K.

24W in a square batten.

Between the 18W and the 40W, and the one that usually turns out to be right - 18 leaves a long room slightly under-lit and 40 overshoots it. Square profile, flat back, surface fixing.

120 lm/W. 3000K and 6500K.
posts.artwork_note: CATALOG.csv calls this the 6FT unit; the artwork's length icon reads 4FT / 1.2M. The caption states no length until that is settled.

posts.caption:
5W, one foot, T5.

The smallest tube in the range. One of these under a wall cabinet lights a worktop without lighting the cook's eyes, which is the entire trick of kitchen task lighting.

1FT / 0.3m, 120 lm/W. 3000K and 6500K.

How the D-shape ships.

Boxed with the date-of-manufacture strip on the end - the part worth photographing before it goes on the shelf, because it is what settles a warranty claim eighteen months later. 40,000 hours rated, one year on the carton.

10W, 1.5FT / 0.45m, 120 lm/W. 3000K and 6500K.

10W in one foot. High power.

Ten watts across 0.3m is a dense little fitting - more output per inch than anything else in the tube range. Display cases, shelf edges, signage returns: short runs where there is no room for length so the watts have to be concentrated.

120 lm/W. 3000K and 6500K.

9W, one foot, square batten.

A watt below the 10W and a different job - this is the general-purpose short batten rather than the high-output one. Cupboards, meter boxes, the inside of a stair bulkhead.

1FT / 0.3m, 120 lm/W. 3000K and 6500K.

5W, one foot. The bottom of the tube range.

Small enough that they get bought in tens rather than ones - sign trays, showcase interiors, mirror surrounds. Square profile so they screw straight to a flat surface with no cradle.

1FT / 0.3m, 120 lm/W. 3000K and 6500K. Wholesale rates on cartons.

7W in the classic A60 shape.

A60 is the ordinary bulb silhouette - 60mm across the widest point, the profile every lampholder and shade in the country was designed around. Which is the whole argument for it: nothing needs to change but the bulb.

E27 or B22. 120 lm/W, AC 85-265V. 3000K and 6500K. Two-year warranty.

24W, BS100.

The BS shape is the wide dome - a bowl rather than a bulb. The broader face puts more emitter area behind the diffuser, which spreads the light instead of concentrating it, and that is what you want from a fitting hanging bare in the middle of a room.

E27 / B22, 120 lm/W. 3000K and 6500K.

30W in a T100.

The T shape is the tall cylinder - straight sides, flat top. It exists because heat rises: a column of aluminium under the diffuser carries the junction heat down to the base, which is how you run 30W out of a fitting this size without cooking it.

E27 / B22, 120 lm/W, AC 85-265V. 3000K and 6500K.

18W, A80.

An A60 grown by two centimetres. Same familiar shape, more room inside for driver and heatsink, which is what lets it carry 18W where the A60 tops out lower. It still goes into an ordinary holder.

E27 or B22, 120 lm/W. 3000K and 6500K. Two-year warranty.

13W, A65.

Five millimetres wider than an A60 and the same in every other respect - it drops into the identical holder and sits under the identical shade. The extra width is heatsink, not decoration.

E27 / B22, 120 lm/W, AC 85-265V. 3000K and 6500K.

32W, BS115. A hall bulb.

The wide-dome shape earns its place in a stairwell or an entrance hall - one fitting, high up, no shade, throwing in every direction. A narrow bulb in that position lights the floor and leaves the walls dark.

E27 / B22, 120 lm/W. 3000K and 6500K.

40W, T115. Shop counter wattage.

Once past about 30W a bulb stops being domestic. This is what goes into a general store, a workshop or a covered market stall - a bare holder, a tall bulb, and enough output that nobody needs a second fitting.

E27 / B22, 120 lm/W, AC 85-265V. 3000K and 6500K.

30W out of an A60 body.

That is a lot of watts in the standard silhouette, and the reason it works is the 120 lm/W figure - the less of the input that turns into heat, the more a small envelope can carry.

E27 / B22, AC 85-265V. 3000K and 6500K. Two-year warranty.

40W in an A80.

The top of the A80 range as a general-service bulb. Familiar shape, 40W behind it - which covers a large room off a single centre fitting where the alternative is running new points.

E27 or B22, 120 lm/W. 3000K and 6500K.

45W, BS125.

125mm across the dome. At this size the bulb is doing the job of a small fitting on its own - which is exactly how it gets used, screwed into a bare holder in a warehouse office or a covered yard.

E27 / B22, 120 lm/W, AC 85-265V. 3000K and 6500K.

50W, T125.

The wide-voltage figure is the one that matters at this size. AC 85-265V means the driver holds regulation through the sag and the surge that a bulb on Pakistani mains sees every day - and voltage swing, not hours, is what kills most of them.

E27 / B22, 120 lm/W. 3000K and 6500K.

40W in the standard A60 envelope.

The shape does the selling here. A customer who wants more light and does not want to hear about fittings can be handed this, and it goes into whatever they already own.

E27 or B22, 120 lm/W, AC 85-265V. 3000K and 6500K. Wholesale rates on cartons.

50W, A80.

Fifty watts inside an eighty-millimetre body is the hardest thermal ask in the bulb range, which is why the base of this one is as much aluminium as the top is diffuser.

E27 / B22, 120 lm/W, AC 85-265V. 3000K and 6500K. Two-year warranty.

60W, BS135. The widest bulb in the range.

135mm across. At this point the argument for a bulb over a fitting is purely practical - it needs no bracket, no driver box and no wiring beyond the holder that is already there.

E27 / B22, 120 lm/W. 3000K and 6500K.

60W, T135.

The tall 60. Where the BS135 spreads its output sideways, the T shape sends more of it straight down - which is what a market stall or a workshop bench wants, and what a domestic ceiling generally does not.

E27 / B22, 120 lm/W, AC 85-265V. 3000K and 6500K.

50W, A60.

The most output the standard bulb shape carries in this range. Anything past it and the envelope has to grow - which is what the A80 and the T-series exist for.

E27 / B22, 120 lm/W, AC 85-265V. 3000K and 6500K.

60W, A80. Two-year replacement warranty.

The warranty is worth stating plainly at the top of a range. A 60W LED bulb runs its driver hard, and what separates a good one from a cheap one is not the first month - it is whether it is still at full output in the second year.

E27 / B22, 120 lm/W, AC 85-265V. 3000K and 6500K.

60W out of an A60.

The hardest thing in the bulb range to build, and the easiest to sell: maximum output in the shape that fits everything. 120 lm/W is what makes it possible at all.

E27 or B22, AC 85-265V. 3000K and 6500K. Two-year warranty. Wholesale and dealer rates on quantity.

13W bubble light. The dome is the point.

A flat downlight puts a disc of light on the floor and leaves a hard edge. The domed diffuser on a bubble sits proud of the ceiling, so it throws sideways as well as down and the room lights evenly instead of in circles.

120mm face, indoor. 120 lm/W. 3000K, 4000K and 6500K.

10W bubble light - small fitting, soft spread.

The softness comes from the depth of the diffuser. Light leaves the emitter, bounces around inside the dome and comes out with no visible source in it, which is why you can sit under one without seeing spots.

120mm face, indoor use. 120 lm/W. 3000K / 4000K / 6500K.

Indoor rated, and what that rules out.

No IP rating on this fitting, which means no bathroom ceiling above a shower, no covered porch, no kitchen directly over a hob. Everywhere else indoors it is fine. Worth saying plainly, because a bubble light going into a wet room is the single most common way one of these comes back.

10W, 120mm face, 120 lm/W. 3000K / 4000K / 6500K.

20W on track. Move it whenever the display moves.

That is the entire argument for track over fixed downlights in a retail space: the stock changes every season, the ceiling does not, and re-aiming a head takes seconds where re-cutting plaster takes a day.

Aluminium body, black. 120 lm/W. 3000K, 4000K and 6500K.

12W track head.

The small one, for close work - a jewellery case, a shelf of small goods, a picture. At 12W you can put four on a two-metre track without the whole wall going flat and shadowless.

Aluminium body, black finish. 120 lm/W. 3000K / 4000K / 6500K.

30W. The top of the track range.

For high ceilings and long throws - a showroom where the track is five metres up and the goods are on the floor. Below about four metres this is usually too much, and the 20W is the one you want.

Aluminium body, black. 120 lm/W. 3000K, 4000K and 6500K.

100W street light. IP65, 140 lm/W, 0.95 power factor.

Three numbers that between them decide whether a street light is worth putting up. IP65 keeps the monsoon out. 140 lm/W is how much of the input reaches the road. 0.95 power factor is why the feeder cable does not have to be sized for a load you are not actually using.

AC 85-265V. 3000K and 6500K.

50W. Lanes, service roads, society streets.

The small street light, and the one most residential schemes should be specifying. A 100W head on a six-metre pole over a narrow lane is not safer - it is glare, and it puts more light on first-floor windows than on the road.

IP65, 140 lm/W, 0.95 pF, AC 85-265V. 3000K and 6500K.

150W, for the main road.

The largest head in the street range. Carriageways, highway service roads, industrial estate approaches - spans where the poles are far enough apart that the light has to reach.

IP65, 140 lm/W, 0.95 power factor, AC 85-265V. 3000K and 6500K.

100W solar street light. Five days of light with no sun.

The specification that matters on a solar head is not the panel, it is the battery chemistry. This one carries a 600WH LiFePO4 pack at 3.2V, rated eight years - lithium iron phosphate rather than the lead-acid that dies in two summers on a pole in this climate.

18V/150W monocrystalline panel, MPPT controller, 4-6 hour charge. Osram 3030 beads, 6000-6500K. Motion sensor, auto on at dusk. IP65, die-cast aluminium.

100W solar flood. 3.2V, 10AH.

Battery capacity is the honest number on a solar flood - it sets how long the thing actually runs after dark, which is the only question anybody is really asking. 10 amp-hours at this wattage carries a normal night.

Die-cast aluminium, 160 lm/W, 6500K. Panel and remote included.

90W solar, for the road with no cable on it.

This is the case solar actually wins: a lane, a farm track, a society street where trenching a feeder costs more than the light. No cable, no meter, no bill - a panel, a battery and a motion sensor that brings it to full output when something moves.

IP65, weather resistant, die-cast body. Auto on at night, auto off in daylight.

200W solar flood, 3.2V / 18AH.

Nearly double the battery of the 100W, because doubling the light and keeping the same pack just means it goes dark at one in the morning. Capacity has to scale with the load or the specification is decorative.

Die-cast aluminium, 160 lm/W, 6500K.

120W. The largest solar street head in the range.

More output means a bigger panel and a bigger pack, and it means the pole has to carry both. Worth checking the bracket before ordering at this size - the weight is not in the light, it is in the panel above it.

Built-in battery, motion sensor, IP65 weather-resistant body. Auto on at dusk.

300W solar flood, 3.2V / 25AH.

The top of the solar range. 160 lm/W is the figure doing the work here - on mains you can be wasteful with efficiency, on a battery every lumen per watt is another twenty minutes before it goes out.

Die-cast aluminium, 6500K. Panel and remote included.

120 LEDs per metre, and 100 metres on a single roll.

One roll covers a full floor of cove lighting without a join. That matters more than it sounds - every splice in a strip run is a future failure point and a visible bright spot on the ceiling.

6.8mm wide, so it drops into a standard aluminium channel. Cuttable, and available in warm white, white, warm natural, blue, pink and green.

288 LEDs a metre. No dots, no hotspots, just one continuous line.

That density is the whole difference between neon flex and a strip behind a diffuser. Pack the emitters close enough and the eye stops resolving them individually - which is why this can be run bare along a wall where a 120 LED/m strip would look like a row of beads.

8mm, 10W per metre, cuttable every 2.5cm. 100m roll. Six colours.

14W a metre, 240 LEDs a metre, cuttable every 4cm.

The brightest strip in the range, and the finest cut interval on a standard strip - 4cm means you can size a run to a shelf or a step almost exactly, instead of losing most of a metre to the nearest cut mark.

Six colours: warm white, white, warm natural, blue, pink, green.

The channel, not the strip.

A silicon profile is what turns a line of visible diodes into a line of light. The strip goes inside, the translucent face diffuses it, and the whole thing bends - which an aluminium channel will not do, so this is what goes round a curved bulkhead or a circular ceiling detail.

Flexible, easy to bend, takes standard strip.

7W a metre, 120 LEDs a metre, cut every metre.

The general-purpose strip. Enough density that it reads as a line rather than a row of points once it is behind a lip, and a metre cut interval that suits ceiling coves, where runs are long and nobody is trimming to the centimetre.

Six colours available.

50 metres of COB neon, cuttable every 2.5cm.

The short roll. 50m is the length that suits signage and shopfronts rather than a whole building - and at 2.5cm cut intervals it will follow lettering, which is what it mostly gets bought for.

High-density COB, so the lit line is continuous. Six colours.

88 LEDs a metre, 70 metres to a roll.

The economy density. Fewer diodes per metre than the 120 version, which shows if it is run bare and does not if it is behind a lip - and on a long cove that is a real saving across the job.

6.8mm, cuttable every metre. Six colours. Wholesale rates on full rolls.

288 LEDs a metre, cut every half metre.

At this density the strip behaves like the neon flex - close enough spacing that the individual emitters stop being visible, so it can go behind a shallow lip without the dotting that gives a cheap install away.

10W per metre. Six colours.

5W a metre. The quiet end of the strip range.

88 LEDs a metre, cut every metre. Not a lighting strip so much as an outline one - under a handrail, along a plinth, round a mirror, where the job is to describe an edge rather than light a room.

Six colours: warm white, white, warm natural, blue, pink, green.

The X182, in black aluminium.

Two curved blades, offset, with the light coming off the inner faces rather than pointing at you. That is the whole design: the fitting is the shade, so what the room gets is a wash up and down the wall and no visible source at eye level.

12W, 960 lm, 3000K warm white. 80% energy saving.

The Marbal - the only wall light in the range rated IP65.

Which makes it the one that goes outside. A porch, a boundary wall, a covered car park - places where every other fitting on this list would take one monsoon and fill with water.

10W, 800 lm, 3000K warm white. White aluminium and PC. 80% energy saving.

X158, black aluminium.

A ring rather than a blade - light emitted around the circumference so the wall behind carries a halo and the fitting itself reads as a dark circle inside it. It wants a plain wall; on patterned paper the effect disappears.

12W, 960 lm, 3000K warm white. 80% energy saving.

The same X182, in white.

Black sconces read as objects on a light wall. White ones nearly disappear into it and leave only the glow - which is the right call in a bedroom, and the wrong one if the fitting is meant to be seen.

12W, 960 lm, 3000K warm white. White aluminium. 80% energy saving.

X897Y, black aluminium, 12W.

3000K on every wall light in this range, and that is deliberate rather than a limitation. A sconce is not a work light - it is there to make a wall look warm at night, and 6500K on a bedroom wall reads as a corridor in a hospital.

960 lm. 80% energy saving.

X158 in white with a dotted aluminium face.

The texture is the difference. Where the black X158 is a solid ring, this one is perforated, so a little of the light comes through the face as well as around it and the fitting itself is lit rather than silhouetted.

12W, 960 lm, 3000K warm white. 80% energy saving.

X960F, 10W, 900 lumens.

The smaller body in the range. Two watts down on the twelves and only sixty lumens behind them, which is the useful part - a narrower fitting for a narrow wall, without the output dropping away with the size.

Black aluminium, 3000K warm white. 80% energy saving.

X155, black aluminium and polycarbonate.

The PC is not a cost saving - it is the diffusing half. Aluminium takes the heat out at the back, polycarbonate softens the light at the front, and the join between them is what stops a 12W emitter reading as a bright point on the wall.

960 lm, 3000K warm white. 80% energy saving.

X960Y, 10W, black aluminium.

The last of the sconces, and the one that pairs with the X960F - same body size, different face. Wall lights sell in pairs and fours rather than singles, because they go either side of a bed or along a corridor, and a range only works if the shapes match across it.

3000K warm white. Wholesale rates on cartons.
